newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania sees two years of falling coffee output.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania sees two years of falling coffee output.

text.p: Capricious weather, crop disease and the psychological impact of a lack of frost in Brazil will force a decline in Tanzania's coffee production for some two seasons, the country's chief coffee official said.

Tanzania Coffee Board (TCB) Managing Director Edward Sannda said that the lack of frost in Brazil had particularly affected local production. Farmers who believed their earnings would rise on a Brazilian frost had now discovered that was not to be.
Erratic distribution of chemicals and fertiliser plus unseasonal rains were also major contributors to a decline in production, he told Reuters in an interview on Monday.
Sannda said many key growing areas had no rain during the flowering season, while disease was prevalent in the highlands.
He forecast production in 1995/96 (Oct-Sept) at 50,000 tonnes, declining to 42,000 in 1996/97. Coffee board figures put 1994/95 output at 55,000 tonnes.
He also saw a fall in earnings in 1995/96 and 1996/97.
"We are expecting a much lower price -- between $1.50 and $2 per kg this year," he said. Comparative prices for 1994/95 were between $2.50 and $3.50 per kg.
Last year, coffee exports earned Tanzania about $140 million but earnings in 1995/96 were set to fall to about $110 million
"Next year (1996/97), earnings would be $90 million -- that is anybody's guess," he said.
Sannda played down recent reports that liberalisation of the Tanzanian coffee industry since 1994 had contributed to a decline in quality.
"This year we've put more effort into quality control at the buying centres to make sure that quality will be taken care of even more."
He said the number of coffee estates under cultivation in Tanzania, which accounted for five percent of total production, was in decline.
Smallholders produce about 95 percent of all coffee in Tanzania.
